strengths: State-of-the-art empirical results across three mathematical competition benchmarks with comprehensive baseline comparisons across multiple model scales

Significant infrastructure innovations achieving 4-5× training speedup through well-motivated asynchronous scheduling, partial rollout, and load balancing techniques that generalize beyond this application
Thorough experimental analysis with strong ablations demonstrating necessity of each refinement stage and showing clear scaling laws from 2k to 300k training samples
Well-engineered three-stage data synthesis pipeline with thoughtful progression through code injection, quality verification, and self-correction injection
Excellent reproducibility with detailed training settings, evaluation protocols, and prompts provided; clear presentation with appropriate technical depth
Demonstrates emergent code self-correction capabilities and shows model naturally scales tool utilization (70%→95%) and invocation frequency with problem complexity
weaknesses: Limited novelty in individual components—relies primarily on existing techniques (GRPO, code injection, verification); main contribution is systems engineering integration rather than fundamental algorithmic advances

Narrow evaluation scope: only three closely-related US high school math competition benchmarks; no assessment on broader mathematical reasoning (GSM8K, MATH) or other tool-use domains; lacks statistical significance testing

Severe reproducibility barriers: requires 128-node distributed cluster and depends on inaccessible DeepSeek-V3 teacher model for data synthesis; no quantified computational costs or feasibility assessment for typical researchers

Insufficient justification for design choices: multi-stage RL progression (48k→72k→96k) appears ad-hoc with 10% threshold chosen arbitrarily; reward formula parameters (α, β, Rmax) not studied; no sensitivity analysis
Incomplete analysis of code execution safety and error handling: timeout behavior not detailed, security considerations unaddressed, verification robustness not discussed

Missing error analysis and failure mode investigation; 'emergent self-correction' claimed but not rigorously quantified; no analysis of when tool use helps vs. hurts or transfer to out-of-distribution settings

Confounded baseline comparisons: different methods use different base models (Qwen3, DeepSeek-Distill, etc.), making it difficult to isolate AgentMath contribution from base model quality; proprietary baselines have unknown training procedures

strengths: Clear motivation addressing three concrete bottlenecks (data scarcity, continuous RL improvement, ultra-long sequence training efficiency) with well-designed solutions

Comprehensive three-stage data synthesis pipeline with thoughtful multi-dimensional quality filtering (format consistency, code executability, environmental feedback alignment, rationality assessment) validated by ablation studies
Strong empirical results competitive with frontier proprietary models: AgentMath-30B-A3B achieves 90.6%/86.4%/73.8% on AIME24/25/HMMT25 across multiple model scales (1.7B-235B parameters)

Rigorous experimental methodology with systematic ablations, data scaling laws (2k-300k samples), multi-scale validation, controlled ReTool comparison under identical settings, and novel IMO-AnswerBench evaluation
Excellent reproducibility: comprehensive implementation details, explicit prompts, training procedures, computational cost analysis (109h/128GPUs), and commitment to open-source code release
Practical systems contributions combining asynchronous scheduling, partial rollouts, and prefix-aware load balancing to achieve 4-5× speedup on ultra-long sequences (96k tokens, 96 tool calls)
Thorough data contamination mitigation through exact matching, 4-gram+MinHash LSH filtering, semantic similarity removal, and validation using base models released before benchmark publication
Demonstrated generalizability beyond mathematics to GPQA (physics/chemistry) achieving 58.9% accuracy, indicating scalability of approach
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: individual components use existing techniques (GRPO for RL, well-known systems optimization techniques); primary contribution is engineering-focused combination rather than fundamental innovations

High computational barrier (109 hours with 128 GPUs; even efficient version requires 76 hours) limits accessibility and reproducibility for most researchers; insufficient cost comparison with competing methods

Heavy dependence on powerful teacher models (DeepSeek-R1/V3, Qwen-30B) creates potential circular dependency and makes it unclear how much improvement stems from data synthesis versus superior teacher knowledge

Limited theoretical or mechanistic understanding of why tool augmentation helps; missing analysis of problem categories where tools hurt performance, failure modes, and when pure reasoning outperforms tool-augmented reasoning

Data contamination concerns persist despite mitigation: AIME24/25/HMMT25 contain only ~30 problems each; semantic similarity filtering removes only top-5 samples; 0.6 n-gram threshold is somewhat arbitrary

Incomplete design justification in main text: segment length rationale (3k tokens), reward hyperparameters (α=0.1, β=0.01), and code complexity filtering (≤5 lines based on 280 manual annotations) appear primarily in appendix
Very dense presentation (53 pages) with critical insights scattered; Table 4 is overwhelming; limited synthesis of key lessons; could distill 3-5 core insights more clearly

Insufficient ablation analysis: What percentage of improvement comes from tools vs. multi-stage refinement? Marginal gains on geometry problems (73.8% vs 71.4%) not thoroughly analyzed; no systematic error categorization
